rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In vocatives, the first-person possessive yāʾ is dropped like tanwīn, since it substitutes for tanwīn in the noun.
rows.anchor: لأن ياء الإضافة في الاسم بمنزلة التنوين لأنها بدل من التنوين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The remaining kasra distinguishes annexation from other forms; omission is common in vocatives, where the kasra suffices and causes no ambiguity.
rows.anchor: فحذف وترك آخر الاسم جرا ليفصل بين الإضافة وغيرها وصار حذفها هنا لكثرة

rows.speaker: بعض العرب
rows.claim: Some Arabs retain the possessive yāʾ in vocatives, as in calls to the Lord and to a people.
rows.anchor: وبعض العرب يقول يا ~~رب اغفر لى ويا قوم لا تفعلوا

rows.speaker: يونس
rows.claim: Yūnus reports retention of the yāʾ in vocatives as a dialect both in pause and in connected speech.
rows.anchor: وثبات الياء فيما زعم يونس في الأسماء

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو
rows.claim: Abū ʿAmr is reported to recite the vocative with the possessive yāʾ retained.
rows.anchor: كان أبو عمرو يقول # يا عبادى فاتقون

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن عبد الأعلى القرشي
rows.claim: A rajaz verse by ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿAbd al-Aʿlā al-Qurashī witnesses retention of yāʾ in the vocative ilāhī.
rows.anchor: وقال الراجز وهو عبد الله بن عبد الأعلى القرشي # % وكنت إذ كنت إلهى وحد كالم %

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some speakers replace the possessive yāʾ with alif because alif is lighter, as in yā rabbā and yā ghulāmā.
rows.anchor: وقد يبدلون مكان ~~الياء الألف لأنها أخف وسنبين ذلك إن شاء الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: At pause, hāʾ is added after the replacement alif to make the otherwise faint alif clearer.
rows.anchor: فإذا وقفت قلت يا غلاماه | وإنما ألحقت الهاء

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Al-Khalīl analyzes the hāʾ in forms such as yā abah as the ordinary feminine hāʾ found in ʿamma and khāla.
rows.anchor: فزعم الخليل رحمه الله أن هذه الهاء مثل الهاء في عمة وخالة

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Al-Khalīl adduces the pause forms yā ummah and yā abah, parallel to yā khālah, as evidence for that analysis.
rows.anchor: ويدلك ~~على أن الهاء بمنزلة الهاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The hāʾ is attached especially in vocatives annexed to oneself as compensation for the deleted yāʾ; this is rare outside the vocative.
rows.anchor: في النداء إذا أضفت إلى نفسك خاصة كأنهم جعلوها عوضا من حذف الياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Vocative hāʾ marks and reinforces attention like yā; this construction is therefore restricted to the vocative.
rows.anchor: ولا يكون هذا في غير النداء لأنهم جعلوها [ تنبيها ] فيها بمنزلة يا

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Al-Khalīl explains feminine hāʾ with masculine father by noting that masculine referents can have feminine names or descriptions, and vice versa.
rows.anchor: وسألت ~~الخليل رحمه الله عن قولهم يا أبه ويا أبت لا تفعل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sībawayh explains abawayn as combining ab and abah, with abah used for a masculine only in vocative; outside it the form is abā, while the feminine is wālida.
rows.anchor: فكأنهم إنما قالوا أبوان لأنهم جمعوا بين أب وأبة

rows.speaker: بعض العرب
rows.claim: Yūnus reports a dialect that says yā umm without hāʾ, treating it like deletion of the hāʾ in Ṭalḥa.
rows.anchor: وحدثنا ~~يونس أن بعض العرب يقول يا أم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The deletion is confined to mother among annexed vocatives; father and mother forms are exceptional because they are frequent, not a general productive rule.
rows.anchor: في النداء كما قالوا يا صاح في هذا الاسم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In nisba formation, final yāʾ or wāw preceded by a consonant remains unchanged because it behaves like a sound consonant.
rows.anchor: في هذا الباب لأنه حرف جرى مجرى غير المعتل

rows.speaker: من الناس
rows.claim: One view forms nisbas from feminine nouns in -iyya with yāʾ, treating the base as a non-defective noun after removing tāʾ marbūṭa.
rows.anchor: وفي ظبية ظبيي وفي دمية دميي وفي فتية فتيي وهو القياس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This yāʾ formation is supported by the behavior of rami and naḥi, which pattern like sound nouns; if Umayya permits it, it is still more apt for ramiya.
rows.anchor: فتجريه مجرى ما لا يعتل نحو درع وترس ومتن

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو
rows.claim: Yūnus reports that Abū ʿAmr used the yāʾ form ẓabiyy for ẓabiyya, which Sībawayh says is the sole analogical form.
rows.anchor: وحدثنا يونس أن ~~أبا عمرو وكان يقول في ظبية ظبيي

rows.speaker: يونس
rows.claim: Yūnus gives an alternative with wāw for ẓabiyya, damiyya, and fatiyya.
rows.anchor: وأما يونس فكان يقول في

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Al-Khalīl explains the wāw forms as analogies to faʿla: the suffixed forms look like that pattern, whose nisba preserves wāw.
rows.anchor: فقال الخليل كأنهم شبهوها حيث دخلتها ~~الهاء بفعلة

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Al-Khalīl prefers the first, yāʾ-based analysis as more analogical and more idiomatic; he cites Zinwi and Baṭṭawi as parallels.
rows.anchor: هذا قول الخليل وزعم ~~أن الأول أقيسهما وأعربهما

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Al-Khalīl excludes ghazwa and ghadwa from the faʿla analogy because their endings do not match it; their nisbas remain ghazwī and ghadwī.
rows.anchor: وقال لا أقول في غزوة إلا غزوي لأن ~~ذا لا يشبه آخره آخر فعلة

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: For ʿurwa the form is ʿarwī; when deletion of tāʾ leaves wāw after a silent consonant, the wāw does not change.
rows.anchor: في عروة إلا عروي لأن فعلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The unchanged wāw after a silent consonant is supported by the nisba Jirwī from Banū Jurwa.
rows.anchor: لم تغير الواو لأن ما قبلها ساكن

rows.speaker: يونس
rows.claim: Yūnus treats yāʾ-root and wāw-root forms alike in this class and also gives ʿarwī.
rows.anchor: وأما يونس فجعل بنات الياء في ذا وبنات الواو ~~سواء ويقول في عروة عروي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For four-letter nouns ending in extra non-tanwin alif, the best nisba is -ī, as in ḥublī and daflī, because the alif is not a root letter.
rows.anchor: فأحسن القول فيه أن تقول حبلي ودفلي لأنها زائدة

rows.speaker: منهم
rows.claim: Another group adds -āwī to distinguish extra final alif from a root alif, paralleling nouns whose final alif is necessarily extra.
rows.anchor: ومنهم من يقول دفلاوي فيفرق بينها وبين التي من نفس الحرف

rows.speaker: منهم
rows.claim: A further group says ḥablawī, treating the alif like a root letter because the word is built on it and matches malhā in pattern.
rows.anchor: ومنهم من يقول ~~حبلوي فيجعلها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sībawayh accepts malhī beside ḥablawī and notes that added and root letters can coincide in nisba when both are fifth.
rows.anchor: فإن قلت في ملهى ~~ملهي لم أر بذلك بأسا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Forms such as madārī follow the pattern of ḥabālā and ʿadhārā, another way additions and root letters converge.
rows.anchor: وكما قالوا مدارى فجاءوا به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qafā does not permit this deletion or extension because it is a three-letter form, not on the pattern of ḥublā.
rows.anchor: قفا وأشباهه ليس بزنة حبلى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jamzā takes jamzī, not jamzawī or jamzāwī, because its weight is heavy and exceeds malhā; the sequential vowels support comparison with ḥubārā.
rows.anchor: وأما جمزى فلا يكون جمزوي ولا جمزاوي ولكن جمزي لأنها ثقلت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Deletion is more acceptable in maʿzā than malhā because its alif is extra; ḥublā still best follows the initially stated form.
rows.anchor: والحذف في معزى أجوز إذ جاز في ملهى

rows.speaker: الشاعر
rows.claim: The poetic line uses Baṣrā, not al-Baṣrī, as Sībawayh explicitly explains its intended form.
rows.anchor: قال الشاعر # % كأنما يقع البصري بينهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The default pronoun hāʾ is ḍamma followed by wāw; this remains the form unless a stated conditioning environment intervenes.
rows.anchor: اعلم أن أصلها الضم وبعدها الواو لأنها في الكلام كله هكذا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After yāʾ or kasra, hāʾ is kasra and its wāw becomes yāʾ: its lightness resembles yāʾ, and kasra triggers the change as in imāla.
rows.anchor: فالهاء تكسر إذا كان قبلها ياء أو كسرة لأنها خفية

rows.speaker: أهل الحجاز
rows.claim: The Hijazis retain ḍamma and wāw in forms such as bihu and dāruhu, and are reported to read the cited phrase that way.
rows.anchor: وأهل الحجاز يقولون مررت بهو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When hāʾ follows plural mīm, the mīm is kasra to avoid ḍamma after kasra, and the hāʾ's following wāw becomes yāʾ.
rows.anchor: في علامة الجمع كسرتها كراهية

rows.speaker: أهل الحجاز
rows.claim: The Hijazis use forms such as ʿalayhumu and bihimu with ḍamma and wāw after plural mīm.
rows.anchor: ومن قال وبدار هو الأرض قال عليهمو مال وبهمو ذلك

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some speakers instead make mīm kasra before the similar yāʾ, while leaving mīm unchanged where it resembles neither yāʾ nor alif.
rows.anchor: وقال بعضهم ~~عليهمو أتبع الياء ما أشبهها

rows.speaker: قوما من ربيعة
rows.claim: Some of Rabīʿa say minhum with hāʾ following kasra even across a still consonant.
rows.anchor: واعلم أن قوما من ربيعة يقولون منهم أتبعوها الكسرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sībawayh calls the Rabīʿa form poor when a consonant separates hāʾ from kasra; when the vowels are distant, the original form is preferable.
rows.anchor: وهذه لغة رديئة إذا فصلت بين الهاء والكسرة

rows.speaker: ناس من بكر بن وائل
rows.claim: Some Bakr b. Wāʾil speakers assimilate hāʾ after kasra because it is a pronoun marker; Sībawayh judges this dialect very poor.
rows.anchor: وقال ناس من بكر بن وائل من أحلامكم وبكم ~~شبهها بالهاء

rows.speaker: الحطيئة
rows.claim: Al-Ḥuṭayʾa's verse witnesses the Bakr dialect form that assimilates the pronoun hāʾ to a preceding kasra.
rows.anchor: قال الحطيئة # % وإن قال مولاهم على جل حادث % من الدهر ردوا فضل أحلامكم ردوا % %

rows.speaker: هارون
rows.claim: Hārūn identifies the ṣād-to-zāy intermediate pronunciation in ḥattā yaṣdura al-riʿāʾ as al-Aʿraj's and Mecca's current reading.
rows.anchor: وزعم ~~هارون أنها قراءة الأعرج

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When hāʾ is preceded by a moving consonant, as in qāḍiyahu, it is not kasra because it is no longer a weak letter like unmovable alif.
rows.anchor: لم تكسر لأنها إذا تحركت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Despite movement, hāʾ remains faint and can count like a still yāʾ or wāw in rhyme, as in khalīluhā and khalīlū.
rows.anchor: في القوافي متحركة بمنزلة الياء والواو الساكنتين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The hāʾ of the feminine demonstrative hādhihi behaves like pronoun hāʾ because both are markers outside the preceding word.
rows.anchor: هاء هذه فإنهم أجروها مجرى الهاء التي هي علامة الإضمار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: At pause the demonstrative hāʾ is deleted, as in bih and ʿalayh; some Arabs also make it silent in connected speech by analogy with plural mīm.
rows.anchor: إلا أن من العرب من يسكن هذه الهاء في الوصل يشبهها ~~بميم عليهم وعليكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The connected-speech variant is attributed to the fixed kasra and frequency of this form; Sībawayh heard hādhihi ummat Allāh with a silent hāʾ from a trusted speaker.
rows.anchor: سمعت من يوثق بعربيته من العرب يقول هذه أمة الله فيسكن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Doubled verbs with final yāʾ follow other defective-yāʾ verbs, not ordinary doubled verbs: the yāʾ behaves like the final of yakhshā or yarmī.
rows.anchor: آخر المضاعف من بنات الياء يجري مجرى ما ليس فيه تضعيف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When the yāʾ is in a position where its movement is obligatory, assimilation is permitted because the final behaves like a sound consonant; assimilation is more common, though the separated form is also Arabic.
rows.anchor: الإدغام جائز فيه لأن اللام

rows.speaker: الشاعر
rows.claim: A poem with ḥayū witnesses deletion of final yāʾ in the plural, parallel to khashaw and akhshaw.
rows.anchor: قال الشاعر # % وكنا حسبناهم فوارس

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some speakers say ḥayū and ʿayū, analogizing the plural to doubled forms found in the singular, dual, and feminine.
rows.anchor: قال بعضهم حيوا وعيوا لما

rows.speaker: الشاعر
rows.claim: The poem ʿayū bi-amrihim, as the dove failed with its egg, witnesses the alternative plural form.
rows.anchor: قال الشاعر # % عيوا بأمرهم كما % % عيت ببيضتها الحمامة %

rows.speaker: يونس
rows.claim: Yūnus reports many Arabs who keep the two yāʾs distinct in ḥayiya al-rajul and ḥayit al-marʾa rather than treating them as ordinary doubled forms.
rows.anchor: وأخبرنا بهذه اللغة يونس

rows.speaker: بعض العرب
rows.claim: Some Arabs pronounce forms such as aʿyāʾ and aḥyiyya distinctly; Sībawayh says concealment is better, though full distinction is also possible.
rows.anchor: وسمعنا بعض العرب يقول أعيياء وأحيية ~~فيبين وأحسن ذلك أن تخفيها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In subjunctive forms such as raʾaytu maʿiyyan and yurīdu an yuḥyiyahu, the yāʾs are not assimilated because the movement is not obligatory; concealment is best, but distinction is allowed.
rows.anchor: وتجعلها بمنزلة المتحركة فهو أحسن وأكثر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qurʾanic wording a-laysa dhālika bi-qādirin ʿalā an yuḥyiya al-mawtā is evidence against assimilation in this environment.
rows.anchor: والدليل على أن هذا لا يدغم قوله عز وجل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Related forms such as maʿiyya, muḥyiyān, maʿiyān, and ḥayyān can be concealed or distinguished; distinction is clearer after kasra because three yāʾs meet.
rows.anchor: والتبيين فيه أحسن مما في يائه كسرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The form taḥiyya follows the pattern tafʿila, like aḥyiyya.
rows.anchor: فأما تحية فبمنزلة أحيية وهي تفعلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Doubled yāʾ is rare because final yāʾ is already heavy and a preceding yāʾ makes it heavier.
rows.anchor: والمضاعف من الياء قليل لأن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The form aḥyā is compared with aḥmad and similar sound-root forms because the preceding fatḥa remains fixed, so doubling behaves like madd and wadda.
rows.anchor: فلما ضاعفت صارت بمنزلة مد وأمد وود

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A question about when something happened can be answered with event-times such as the pilgrims' departure, star-setting, or a person's succession.
rows.anchor: وذلك قولك متى سير عليه ؟ فيقول مقدم الحاج وخفوق النجم وخلافة فلان

rows.speaker: بني تميم
rows.claim: Banū Tamīm allow إذا جاء غد فأتني with كان omitted; its expanded sense refers to whatever state of safety or affliction obtains tomorrow.
rows.anchor: غدا فأتنى وهى لغة بنى تميم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The omitted كان is understood from the context and is dropped for ease because كان is frequent and serves as the basic expression for past and future.
rows.anchor: فى كلامهم لأنه الأصل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other frequent expressions also omit understood material, as in ḥīnaʾidhin al-ān and the idiom lā ʿalayka.
rows.anchor: وحذفوا كما ~~قالوا حينئذ الآن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lā ʿalayka omits lā baʾsa or lā ḍarra because the addressee understands the fixed expression; Sībawayh says this ellipsis is confined to that phrase.
rows.anchor: ولا يكون هذا فى غير لا عليك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The explicit إذا كان غدا فأتني is grammatical when prior context has introduced an affair, and this type of ellipsis works with any verb after its overt antecedent.
rows.anchor: لأنك إنما أضمرت بعد ما ذكرت مظهرا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: إذا كان الليل فأتني is not valid in the same way unless night means the entire night or the omitted matter has already been introduced in context.
rows.anchor: فإن قلت إذا كان الليل فأتنى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For a particular night or day, sahar and similar temporal names occur only as accusative adverbs; sahar can inflect when indefinite or with the article, and its diminutive is sahīr.
rows.anchor: ومما لا يحسن فيه إلا النصب قولهم سير عليه سحر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When denoting the particular day, ḍuḥā and ʿashiyya are adverbial accusatives and do not take genitive in this use, as in the verse's comparison to an evening or its morning.
rows.anchor: ضحى يومك لأنهما لا يتمكنان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Names such as dhāta marratin, buʿaydāta bayn, and bakran are likewise restricted to adverbial accusative in these senses, not ordinary nominal use.
rows.anchor: ذات مرة نصب لا يجوز إلا هذا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other specific time expressions, including ḍaḥwa, ʿatma, dhāta yawm, dhāta layl, laylan, and nahāran, behave similarly as adverbs.
rows.anchor: وكذلك سير عليه عتمة إذا أردت

rows.speaker: العرب
rows.claim: Yūnus reports the normal Arabic use of dhā ṣabāḥ like dhāta marratin; Khathʿam has a differing dialect that permits it to be raised.
rows.anchor: أخبرنا بذلك يونس عن العرب

rows.speaker: لخثعم
rows.claim: A Khathʿam speaker uses dhā ṣabāḥ outside the ordinary adverbial pattern, as in a verse permitting nominative case.
rows.anchor: وقال رجل من خثعم ~~PageV01P226 # % عزمت على إقامة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A non-inflecting temporal expression cannot be made a raised subject at the start of a sentence unless it is construed as an adverb.
rows.anchor: وجميع ما ذكرنا من غير المتمكن إذا ابتدأت اسما لم يجز

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Al-Khalīl says that words following lā can take the case of their syntactic position rather than the case imposed directly by lā; Dhu al-Rumma's example illustrates this.
rows.anchor: فزعم الخليل ~~رحمه الله أن هذا يجرى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The same positional case appears in the poetic phrase falsnā bil-jibāli wa-lā al-ḥadīdā, where the poet uses the syntactic position rather than the governing particle.
rows.anchor: ولا الحديدا % % أجراه على الموضع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sībawayh explains that qalīlun and kathīrun are raised by syntactic position in the expression lā māla lahu.
rows.anchor: مال له قليل ولا كثير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After lā, as in lā mithlahu rajul, one may follow the syntactic position, follow lā with tanwīn and accusative, or use the construction lā mithlahu rajulan.
rows.anchor: إذا حملته على الموضع كما قال بعض العرب

rows.speaker: ذو الرمة
rows.claim: Dhu al-Rumma's line lā amthāluhunna layāliyā supplies a poetic example of the case variation after lā.
rows.anchor: وقال ذو الرمة # % هى الدار إذ مى لاهلك جيرة % ليالى لا أمثالهن لياليا % %

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Al-Khalīl argues that lā rajul occupies the position of a nominative subject, as shown by lā rajulun afḍalu minka, equivalent to Zayd is better than you.
rows.anchor: وقال الخليل رحمه الله يدلك على أن لا رجل

rows.speaker: جرير
rows.claim: Jarīr's lā ka-l-ʿashiyyati zāʾiran wa-mazūran must be accusative because evening cannot be a visitor; an implicit verb such as arā is understood.
rows.anchor: من قبل أن العشية ليست بالزائر وإنما أراد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In this construction kāf is a preposition, not a noun, with a sense like fī al-yawm; the omitted verb is understood from frequent usage, as in exclamatory expressions.
rows.anchor: فكاليوم كقولك في اليوم لأن الكاف ليست باسم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In lā ka-l-ʿashiyyati ʿashiyyatan and lā ka-Zaydin rajulun, the second term can be nominative by position because it repeats or classifies the first; lā ka-Zayd means no one like Zayd.
rows.anchor: لأن الآخر هو الأول ولأن

rows.speaker: امرؤ القيس
rows.claim: Imruʾ al-Qays's phrase wa-lā ka-hādhā alladhī fī al-arḍ maṭlūb is understood as wa-lā shayʾun ka-hādhā, with nominative by position; accusative is also possible.
rows.anchor: قال [ الشاعر ] امرؤ القيس # % ويلمها في هواء الجو طالبة %

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The cited mرفad line can be analyzed with an omitted lā aḥad and the following noun related to Zayd, or by analogy with lā māla lahu qalīlan wa-lā kathīran.
rows.anchor: كأنه قال لا أحد كزيد رجلا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lā ʿalayka omits an understood noun, meaning lā baʾsa ʿalayka or lā shayʾa ʿalayka, because the expression is frequent.
rows.anchor: وإنما يريد لا بأس عليك ولا شئ عليك
